note: Number columns are accounting conventions, never people: no commentator produced a number for this population. The authors section is text: what each argues, what the claim is about, the convention in this ledger that comes closest (if any) and why it is not the same thing. External links live in sources.json, keyed to the ids used here. The preset marked central is the page's reference case. A setting reads a number through value_from (a name, or a list of names for a band): a plain name is a field of derived/scaling_check.json, and responses.<path> reads the adopted responses that the corrections payload carries (main_case_2026_09_26/derived/corrections.json meta.responses). A setting's cite lists ids in sources.json; the build refuses an id the registry lacks or one that does not name the convention among its places. A {published:<profile>} token in any string becomes the cost band the September 20 account published for that service profile (model.json meta.headline), and a {response:<name>} token the adopted response band (general_government, school), so no result is typed by hand.

presets.label: CBO-informed central case
presets.summary: The ledger carries the data corrections: a dataset audit, four outside checks and a consumption key corrected for saving and remittances. School spending follows enrollment {response:school}, colleges and other services fully, roads and parks not at all. General government grows with the population as administration spending does across the states, at {response:general_government} of average cost. Both responses are what removing a group of this size saves, a little more than the marginal rates they come from. Police, courts and prisons are charged by use, and the part of free hospital care the account under-charged is keyed to uninsured use. Defense, interest on existing debt and business subsidies are held fixed. The gain from the group's work is counted.
presets.scope_note: Since the evening of 2026-09-26 the adopted main case charges schools at their full average cost per pupil (decisions/2026-09-26-main-case-schools-full-cost.md); this page shows the case adopted earlier that day, which that decision keeps as the one-year budget scenario. The finite-removal responses and the consumption key were adopted on 2026-09-26 (decisions/2026-09-26-main-case-finite-removal-and-consumption-key.md; main_case_2026_09_26/RESULT.md), on top of the data corrections adopted on 2026-09-24 (decisions/2026-09-24-main-case-audit-and-outside-checks.md; main_case_2026_09_24/RESULT.md) and the three changes adopted on 2026-09-23 (decisions/2026-09-23-main-case-general-government-and-use-keys.md; main_case_2026_09_23/RESULT.md). Switching the data corrections off keeps the responses, so it shows these conventions on the data as the account published them, a case no decision adopted. It replaces the September 20 central case, {published:cbo_category_lag_non_school_full} bn, which stays beside it as a preset. Two of its conventions rest on CBO: the rules for who bears each tax, and the school figure, which this repo derives from a CBO regression; the corrections also key income taxes with CBO's income shares. The general-government range is long-run evidence about scale across the states, not a measured response to this group. Both responses assume a cost that is a power of population or enrollment; with a fixed cost plus a constant marginal cost, a removal would save only the marginal rates, $4.1bn less at the low end and $3.4bn less at the high end. Holding defense and interest at zero is this account's assumption.

settings.label: Data corrections
settings.note: A dataset audit and four outside checks (2026-09-24), and the consumption key corrected for saving and remittances (2026-09-26). Tax records by legal status and survey fill-ins, and CBO's income shares, lower the taxes assigned to the group, and the consumption key raises its share of consumption taxes; Treasury's credit shares, program records for benefits and medical care charged by use lower the spending keyed to it. Three corrections that fit no single line (schools priced where the group enrolls, a re-keyed college share, and care work, shelter and audit items) stand as lines of their own at the foot of the spending ledger.

settings.label: School spending
settings.note: CBO's state panel: spending per pupil grows 0.37 points slower for each point of enrollment growth, and 0.34 points faster for each point of decline, so at the margin total school spending moves 63-66% as much as enrollment. The group holds 17.5% of pupils, and when cost is a power of enrollment, removing a share that large saves more than the marginal rate: {response:school} of average cost. These are two point values; the range covers both.

settings.label: General government
settings.note: Tax collection, financial management and state and local administration grow as they do across the states. At the low end the federal executive and legislature stay fixed and federal tax collection grows as financial administration does; at the high end all of it grows at the rate for administration. The group is 12% of residents, and when cost is a power of population, removing a share that large saves more than each part's marginal rate, so the response is {response:general_government} where the rates give 0.59-0.84.

standing.title: Whose ledger is this?
rows: This page. The taxes the group pays, the benefits and services it draws, and the gain from its work that reaches everyone else.
What they earn here against what they would earn elsewhere, known as the place premium. It is inside US GDP but not in this ledger, and it is where most of any world-GDP gain sits.
Effects on countries of origin: money sent home, workers departed.
standing.text: Claims about world GDP add all three. They cannot be netted against this page's number without deciding how much a dollar to a migrant counts against a dollar to someone already here, which is a moral weight, not a measurement. Interest on US debt would never be deducted from world GDP: it is a payment from taxpayers to bondholders, a transfer, and no output is lost. Inside this ledger it is held fixed because debt already issued does not shrink when a population is smaller.

authors.name: Noah Smith
argues: He cites CBO's July 2024 projection: the 2021-26 surge lowers covered federal deficits by about $0.9tn over 2024-2034. CBO's headline excludes discretionary appropriations and state and local budgets.

In his own words the same arrivals are "a long-term fiscal problem, because these people will require heavy government support for their health care, housing, and education; this will end up coming from city and state governments".
authors.object: A recent surge of all origins, the federal budget, a ten-year window.

closest.why: A claim about the federal budget does not charge schools or police, which are almost entirely state and local. He names that local cost himself and does not net it against the federal gain. The repo's September revision no longer calls this a contradiction.

leaves_out: The second generation: 'no mention of the second generation' (scorecard :35). Most of this population is US-born.
A number for the gain from production or complementary skills: none is recorded.

authors.name: Matthew Yglesias
argues: He states no fiscal number in his own voice. The CBO material on Slow Boring is in guest posts (Kolko, 2024-09-12; Elmendorf and Williams, 2023-08-28).

His case is scale and growth, lower grocery and service prices, and hours freed for high-wage women. On cost he has one aside, in a sentence about housing: the tools to end housing shortages, "like immigration", "would cost taxpayers nothing". He concedes congestion costs (traffic, rent, water, pollution) and that crime counts rise with population.
authors.object: Immigrants 'of virtually all stripes', national scale, no stated horizon.

closest.why: This is the condition under which immigration "would cost taxpayers nothing" holds in this ledger. That is an inference from his aside; he did not argue it. His price channel is outside the account (see the objections section).

leaves_out: Local budgets: 'He addresses wages, not local budgets' (audit :67).
The National Academies 2016 report, and any federal, Social Security or debt number of his own (audit :138-139).

authors.name: Bryan Caplan
argues: A moral presumption in favor of free migration, and an economic case that is 'extremely strong': very large global gains from moving labor to productive places. The 'double world GDP' figure is sourced to openborders.info, not to a sentence of his.
Restrictions 'are not necessary to protect American taxpayers': fiscal effects are modest, and where they are not, cheaper keyhole remedies exist (entry fees, surtaxes, exclusion from benefits).
authors.object: Future entrants under open borders; the welfare of migrants and the world as well as natives.

closest.why: No setting of this ledger represents his claim, so no number is shown. His large gains accrue mainly to the migrants themselves (the second row of the table above), and his keyhole remedy applies to future entrants: it cannot be applied to a resident population that is mostly US-born citizens. Switching benefits off in this ledger would only stop counting {assigned:benefits} bn of costs; it would not be his argument.

leaves_out: School, shelter and service load on state and local budgets: what survives an exclusion from welfare (audit :288). The audit's verdict on the taxpayer claim: 'Federal gains can coexist with state/local costs in education, shelter, and related services'.
The cost and feasibility of the keyhole instruments themselves (audit :216).

authors.name: Nicholas Decker
argues: 'Immigrants must make us richer': "I think the assumption of constant returns to scale is nonsense. Not only that, it is obvious nonsense… There are three main channels by which returns simply have to be increasing: specialization, ideas, and fixed costs… of course immigrants make us richer."
authors.object: All immigrants; the total income of people already here; no horizon or cost convention stated.

closest.why: His argument has a production side and no fiscal side. But this ledger's production model has constant returns, the assumption he rejects, so its near-zero private gain is this account's result and not a test of his claim. The repo has withdrawn two of its own earlier rebuttals of him.

leaves_out: Every fiscal line: the audits record him compressing the question into 'one production-function dispute' (audit 2026-04-11 :255-256).
Composition: his July 2026 proposal to rank visas concedes that composition decides the sign (scorecard :79).
